question: Is a heavier padel racket associated with more upper-body injuries in amateur players?
reference_answer: Yes: in a survey of 950 amateur players, using a racket of 350 g or more was associated with the appearance of upper-body injuries (an association, not proven cause); shape, core, overgrips and composition were not.

question: How many amateur players answered the survey on racket characteristics and upper-body injuries and how many of them were women?
reference_answer: 950 amateur players: 803 men and 147 women, from 12 countries.

question: Was racket shape associated with getting injured in amateur padel players?
reference_answer: No. Shape (p = 0.250), core type, number of overgrips and composition were not associated with the appearance of injuries; only racket weight was.

question: How many hours of padel per week were linked to more injuries in amateur players?
reference_answer: Playing more than six hours a week was associated with more injuries (also having less than five years of experience).

question: Which racket shapes did male and female amateur players tend to use?
reference_answer: Men used diamond-shaped rackets more (35.9%), women used round rackets more (44.2%); teardrop was used similarly (39.7% vs 33.3%).

question: What injury incidence rates does the systematic review of padel injuries report?
reference_answer: 3 injuries per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1000 matches, with an overall prevalence of 40%-95%.

question: How many studies and participants did the systematic review on padel injuries include?
reference_answer: Eight studies with 2022 participants (75% male).

question: What is the most frequently reported specific injury diagnosis in padel according to the systematic review?
reference_answer: Tennis elbow, i.e. common extensor tendinopathy (lateral epicondylitis).

question: Why might padel players get so many elbow tendon injuries according to the systematic review?
reference_answer: Possible reasons: many overhead shots and repetitive movements, continuous eccentric contractions when slowing the incoming ball, a stringless racket so tension is not regulated, and rare double-handed backhands.

question: In the study by Sanchez Alcaraz-Martinez, what share of padel injuries happened in training versus competition?
reference_answer: 58% during training and 42% during competition.

question: Where along the racket is the sweet spot of padel rackets located?
reference_answer: Across 225 rackets, all sweet spots lay between 118 and 147 mm from the top of the racket, with an average of 134 mm.

question: Do round padel rackets really have a wider sweet spot?
reference_answer: Not established: the study found no clear correlation between the sweet spot and shape, mass, balance or inertia, so identifying round rackets with wide sweet spots is uncertain; the sweet spot has to be measured.

question: What kind of sweet spot should low-level players choose to avoid injuries?
reference_answer: Rackets with a wide sweet spot, because hitting outside the sweet spot brings extra effort to the arm.

question: How did the researchers measure where the sweet spot of a padel racket is?
reference_answer: A robot hit the racket 90 times along its central line (from 40 to 220 mm from the top, 2 mm steps, repeated three times) while an accelerometer at the handle measured vibration; the sweet spot is where the vibration severity V is minimum.

question: Is the sweet spot of a racket the same as its center of percussion?
reference_answer: No. In the beechwood bar test the sweet spot was at 124 mm while the center of percussion lay between 132 and 150 mm.

question: What are the maximum dimensions allowed for a padel racket?
reference_answer: Total length (head plus handle) at most 45.5 cm, width at most 26 cm, thickness at most 38 mm; the handle at most 20 cm long, 50 mm wide and 50 mm thick.

question: What was the weight range of the 137 padel rackets measured in the inertia study?
reference_answer: From 316 g to 387 g, with a mean of 363 g; balance between 246 and 283 mm (mean 265.5 mm).

question: What does a racket's moment of inertia around the vertical axis tell the player?
reference_answer: It determines the stability of the racket when the ball hits off-center: higher inertia increases the racket's resistance to twisting.

question: Did players' feel match the maneuverability index proposed for padel rackets?
reference_answer: Mostly: of 50 users, 91% rated the 0.90-index racket as high maneuverability and 68% rated the 1.12 racket as low; the medium (1.02) racket was harder to classify (59% medium).

question: What materials are used for the core of padel rackets?
reference_answer: Rubber cores such as EVA (black, soft, ultra-soft), foam cores, polyethylene, or hybrids such as EVA plus PE.

question: What VO2max values have been measured in padel players?
reference_answer: Between 38.4 and 55.64 mL/kg/min depending on sex and level.

question: What share of total match time is actual play in high-level padel?
reference_answer: 45.92% of total match time, with rallies of about 12.7 s and breaks of about 14.95 s (work:rest 0.84).

question: What court modification helps children learning padel and what does it change?
reference_answer: Reducing the court from 20 x 10 m to 10 x 6 m increases wall shots, volleys and overhead shots in young beginners.

question: What are the most common injuries in under-18 padel players?
reference_answer: Low back pain (23.3%), knee sprains, plantar fasciitis and elbow injuries (10%), and wrist, ankle and shoulder sprains (6.7%).

question: What kind of racket did most Portuguese padel practitioners in the injury survey use?
reference_answer: Most used light rackets (50.9%) with a carbon-fibre outer shell (76.3%), a soft core (35.9%), a teardrop shape (42.5%) and a single overgrip (61.0%).

question: Was the number of overgrips on the handle associated with injuries in Portuguese padel players?
reference_answer: Yes, weakly: the number of overgrips showed a small positive correlation with injuries in the past year (r = 0.119, p <= 0.05), i.e. more overgrips went with more recent injuries.

question: What injury prevalence did the study of padel players in Madinah find for women and for men?
reference_answer: 44.6% of women versus 8.2% of men reported injuries while playing padel (305 players: 193 men, 112 women).

question: Which lifestyle factors were linked to injury risk among padel players in Madinah?
reference_answer: Stress (94.8% of respondents) was the main one, then physical activity levels (75.7%), diet and nutrition (72.8%), smoking (71.8%), poor sleep quality (50.2%) and previous injuries (46.9%).

question: What equipment choices does the 2026 scoping review recommend to prevent padel injuries?
reference_answer: Individualised equipment: footwear suited to multidirectional movement, a suitable grip size and tackiness, and a racket whose weight and balance are adapted to the player and technical level, to limit wrist/forearm strain.

question: Which body region do the amateur-player survey and the systematic review each identify as the most affected by injuries?
reference_answer: The amateur survey (upper body only) found the shoulder and elbow most affected (elbow about 35%); the systematic review found the elbow the most frequently reported injury site in all five studies that gave joints.

question: What injury rate per 1000 hours did Garcia-Fernandez et al. find and how does the systematic review summarise incidence?
reference_answer: Garcia-Fernandez et al.: 2.75 injuries per 1000 h of padel exposure; the systematic review summarises about 3 injuries per 1000 h of training and 8 per 1000 matches.

question: Is racket weight linked to injuries and is it linked to where the sweet spot is?
reference_answer: Rackets of 350 g or more were associated with more upper-body injuries in amateurs, but no correlation was found between racket weight and sweet spot position.

question: How heavy are padel rackets in lab measurements and what share of male and female amateurs use rackets of 350 g or more?
reference_answer: 137 rackets weighed 316-387 g (mean 363 g); 84.8% of male and 63.9% of female amateur players used rackets of 350 g or more.

question: What does a racket's balance point correlate with and does it predict the sweet spot position?
reference_answer: Balance distance correlates strongly with the moments of inertia around the x and y axes (r = 0.82 and 0.80), but it is not possible to correlate balance with the sweet spot position.

question: How is racket shape linked to playing style and which shapes do male and female amateurs prefer?
reference_answer: Diamond rackets tend to have higher balance (attack/power), round lower balance (control/defence), teardrop in between, though shape is less important than the physical features; men prefer diamond and women round rackets.

question: How does the injury incidence per 1000 hours found in Portugal compare with the systematic review of padel injuries?
reference_answer: Portugal: 3.4 injuries per 1000 h of exposure for the whole sample (6.1 among injured players); the systematic review: about 3 per 1000 h of training and 8 per 1000 matches, so they are similar.
